we’re getting a new cat today. what should i put in her acclimation room? hello,

today, my mom and i are adopting a cat that needs rehoming. we live in an apartment on the second floor and we only have 3 closed rooms, one of which is my bedroom, which is going to be the acclimation room for the new kitty. she is an adult and very sweet. i already have 2 cats at my dad’s house, one we adopted when i was too little to remember, and the other i got for my thirteenth birthday, which, honestly, i don’t really remember the details of how we acclimated him.

i’m in college right now, so i won’t be in there to bother her much (why we chose it), but i’ve come home to help the new cat get settled in. my question is, what should we put in there?

it has my bed, my dresser, and a screen door to my balcony, though we won’t be letting her out on it, but she can definitely listen to the birds and have fresh air. i know we’re supposed to put the food, water, and litter box in there, yes?

there is a lot of space under my bed for her to hide if she wants, but i also have some empty boxes from moving in. it is a fairly small room, about 10 x 10 ft. should i put them on the floor for her? what other additions should i put into the room for her to acclimate?

thank you!

How do I potty train kittens? (3.5 weeks old) So, ill start by saying I'm 16. I dony plan to keep a whole litter, but im fostering for my mom's ex boyfriend and I get to keep one of them. This is my responsibility, which was my decision, so minimal adult intervention.

I know kittens are easy to potty train, put em in, bury their feet, but I think from watching their mom eat her dry food, theyve got it in their heads that its food! I took one, put her paws in the litter and dug in, but soon as I let go, she started eating it! I stopped her, and none of the cats have had problems, but they wont use the litter box right! Ive moved it away so they cant CONTINUE, but id rather they not crap all over my floor.

Should I try and move mama's litterbox closer to them so she can model for them? I have limited space so id rather not

[[EDIT]] I've gotten tons of great advice on this post and im very grateful. I wanted to mention some things and say what I plan on doing.

for one, I'm in school, so I cant constantly watch them, but their mother is there. two, the litter i have is non-clumping but has larger chunks.

as for steps im taking, I'm getting pine pellets as soon as I can for the cats, and I'll put off training. also, multiple people mentioned "the kitten lady" so ill look into some of her content too!​

What works for us: medicating cat Right now I am having to medicate all three of our cats for a month. They are each taking something different - different forms and doses, etc. it’s a bit crazy

Thankfully, the youngest eats anything. So no issues. The oldest is pretty easy going and we are using a pill popper on him. We approach when napping, offer him churo, then do the pill and follow immediately with remaining churo. Seems to be going ok, just once a day - nice. One and done!✅

Last though, is our barely able to handle cat. Can’t pick up, startles easily, needs everything to be “just right”. I’m thankful
Our vet is working with us- we have our med in two forms: liquid compound flavored marshmallow/duck and compounded pill into something called a “tiny tab”.

What has worked is:
- pick up all dry food that is normally out. If we don’t do this, troublesome kitty will NOT eat offered treats or wet food with meds ever.
- morning is: open FRESH can of extra stinky friskies. Ive found a few that are more readily eaten. I squirt his meds in a tiny cup, pour juice out of food and add a tiny bit of food. Mix up and put on a tray for him. He eats it! It MUST be fresh though!
- then i offer him some of his kibble which he will gobble up and put it away when he’s finished.
- 5pm : feed him greenies treats where i have drilled Out a tiny hole I fill with little tiny pieces of the pill stuffed in. It takes about 10 greenies? Sometimes the pill gets spit out so I have extra greenies lined up already drilled with a hole 😂

Then he gets his kibble again, and I pick it up before we go to bed.

That’s it!! Only 20 more days to go… 😵‍💫

Common Health Problems Of Cats If you are new to owning a cat, you may be surprised to find that health problems are a common thing. No matter what breed of cat you own, health problems are to be expected. Some can be hereditary, while others can be easily avoided.

Worms Regardless of the breed of cat, worms are a very common and recurring problem. Tapeworms, roundworms and hookworms are among the most common that infect cats. Cats that have weight gain problems, flea problems, or if you find white spots in his stool, you should ask your veterinarian to test him for worms. Although they can be treated with medication, worms can prove fatal if left untreated.

Hair balls Hairballs are the most common health problem for cats. All cats groom themselves daily, normally swallowing the loose hairs that come from their coats. Occasionally, these loose hairs will gather in a ball and lodge in the digestive tract instead of passing through your cat's stool. When your cat starts coughing and hacking, it normally spits out a hairball. Although it can be rather disgusting in the end, most cats can dislodge the hairballs without any problems.

In rare cases, a hairball can pass through the intestine of a cat, creating a blockage. Blockages are very serious problems and can be life-threatening if left untreated. If your cat becomes constipated, does not eat properly, or has a very dull coat, it could have a blockage. If you notice any of these symptoms, you should immediately take him to the veterinarian. You can prevent hairballs and blockages by brushing your cat 2 or 3 times a week to remove loose hair. You can also give him food designed to control the hairballs.

Urinary tract infection Urinary tract infection is also a common health problem in cats. Urinary tract infection is more common in male cats that have not been sterilized, although females can also suffer from this problem. When a cat suddenly stops going to its litter box, this problem is normally the cause. Another symptom is when the cat's urine begins to smell very strongly. If you suspect that your cat has a urinary tract infection, you should take it to the vet. Your veterinarian can treat the problem with medication and make recommendations to help avoid this problem in the future.

Feline leukemia In the past, feline leukemia was the biggest cause of death in cats. These days however, there are vaccines available that can treat the disease. To treat the disease, your cat will need to receive the vaccine before being exposed. Even if death does not occur immediately, cats exposed to feline leukemia normally have a long lifespan. If you know that your cat has feline leukemia, you should never allow other cats around him, as the virus is very contagious.

To protect your cat, you should always make sure to take her to the vet for her regular checkups. If you keep him informed of his vaccinations, he should lead a healthy and productive life. Although some health problems can be prevented, most of them can. You can also keep your cat indoors, which will protect it from the majority of health problems. If your cat is an outdoor cat, regular visits to the veterinarian will keep it healthy. As long as you take your cat to the vet and keep it healthy, it will be your companion for years to come.

If you like visite or youtube channel we have more videos: cats problems

Can I ask for ideas to train/retrain my cat? Hi all.

I'm at a bit of a loss with my cat, a 5 year old Maine Coon. Male/neutered.

We used to live in a big house - 2 floors + furnished basement - where he could run around the whole place. We've had to move into a smaller apartment, and he doesn't understand we don't own the entire building. He hates closed doors, and keeps clawing/meowing at the door to be let out into the hallway, and once there he wants to go into other people's apartments. We obviously cannot let him do that. We give him walks in the hallway when we can, but he gets into moods where all he wants is to be in the hallway, meowing for hours on end. It can't be healthy for him.

We've tried training him to get used to closed doors, make sure to give him food water, his favorite window, etc with the door closed, and he loses his mind over it. When he gets into a mood we try to distract him with toys, pets, food, but he wants nothing to do with anything else once he sets his mind on it. The apartment door is all scratched up from him trying to get out.

I don't know what to try here. How can we get through to him that some doors are closed to him, that he can't live in the hallway?

How to help my very fearful kitten acclimate Hello! I just got a new kitten from a shelter about a week ago, and he is the sweetest little thing but is SO afraid of everything. He’s about 8-9 weeks old so I understand it will take some time.

We have a house of 1 full grown cat (he likes her already, so we’re doing well on that front) and 3 large dogs. We’ve been keeping him in a bathroom for the time being to let him get used to the sounds/smells of our house, and introduced our existing cat a couple of days ago with much success.

I’ve also started letting him sleep on my lap while I’m relaxing at the end of the day, and the dogs are present so he is slowly being introduced that way with me as a safe space for him. He does pretty well with that.

However, anytime we bring him to a new room he trembles and if he is put down will hide with no intention of coming out to explore. I don’t expect him to be okay with the dogs or the whole house right away especially considering how recently he was brought home. But I’m concerned about introducing new things too fast or too slow. I guess I’m mostly wondering if we should keep him in the room he’s comfy in and keep doing these slow introductions to new rooms or if we should let him out and let him hide until he’s comfortable? Or maybe move him to a new room and let him acclimate to a single room at a time with the main living space being last for the sake of not having to be around the dogs for now? I’ve never had a fearful cat, all I’ve raised so far have been confident from the start. Any advice is welcome!

How long to acclimate to outdoors? Back in January, we had an approximate 1yo female cat adopt us. She would come inside a few hours in the evening for dinner, and then go back out for the rest of the time. She was pregnant unbeknownst to us. The kittens were born in March, and we still have one. The mama was spayed in July, and kitten was neutered in October. He has been inside the whole time. I’ve been leash training him with a harness. How long should I keep training him until he’ll be ready to explore on his own or with his mama?

I’m not sure what to do with my sick, difficult cat. Not asking for medical advice.

My baby, Arabella, has been with me since she was a year old. We are VERY bonded. She is now 11. She’s generally been healthy, but in the past year, I’ve spent a couple grand towards some minor health issues. However, in that, some bigger concerns have come up. Without going into too much detail, she has no official diagnosis yet, and she acts normal, happy and healthy; her blood work suggests otherwise. Her ultrasound did not show anything serious. The method the vet has taken is treat with medicine and see if it works.

A few months ago, the first time I was given a bunch of meds for her, to be administered multiple times a day, I had a trip for a few days already booked out of the country. My husband couldn’t get the cat to take her pills. My friend, who has pet sit many cats and given them meds, could get her to take them the first day I was gone, but then my cat got very aggressive. Both my husband and friend could not get her to take them. She ended up going off them for a few days (vet okayed this) until I came back.

Those meds did not solve the problem. Months later, the vet is prescribing a month of antibiotics and steroids multiple times a day for a couple months, then steroids once a day for life.

She will take pills from no one but me. We have lots of expensive travel plans booked. Of course we have sitters for all those times for her and my other cat, but I know we will not get someone able to give her her pills multiple times a day.

Am I just not able to leave the house for the rest of her life? We don’t even know if this medication will work.

I feel evil and guilty and ashamed but I’m not sure if I have any options other than to cancel thousands of dollars worth of vacations, booked before we knew about these meds, and being in my cousin’s wedding. And never leave the house for a night until she passes. Is it time to say goodbye sooner and just enjoy her while I can? I feel horrible at the option but it feels like the most obvious versus putting her through stress of someone wrangling her to shove pills down her throat multiple times a day.

Has anyone been in this position before, and what did you do? The vet was no help when I explained her aggression towards our pet sitter.

One of my former friends recently passed away and now I have his cat. I'm looking for advice on methods for having the cat adapt to my home that would be the most comfortable/least stressing for him I used to have a childhood friend, let's call him A. A and I grew up together from Grades 0-12 and stayed in contact during college. Unfortunately we ended up no longer being friends, due to something unforgivable they did. I was not in contact with them for about two years because of this.
I have now found out A recently passed away from an illness. I also learned that A wrote me into their will as the beneficiary for Rotisserie Chicken(not their real name), after I was contacted by their lawyer.
A was from an abusive home and left their family years ago.
Their cat Rotisserie Chicken was adopted when they were a kitten. Rotisserie Chicken suffered from A's parents too so they ended up being terrified of anyone other than A, me, and my partner.
The only reason Rotisserie Chicken is fine with me is because A often brought Rotisserie Chicken over to my home frequently, well before they were first attacked. So with A being friendly with me + me treating Rotisserie Chicken well (with various bribes too), Rotisserie Chicken grew quite fond of me.
As for my partner, Rotisserie Chicken also has known them for a long time. My house was our hangout spot.

The point of this is that Rotisserie Chicken gets incredibly stressed, frightened, ill, and violent towards anyone other than us three.

A has had various partners or friends come over through their house and if they stay too long Rotisserie Chicken's physical / mental health struggles severely because of his stress.

Strangely Rotisserie Chicken is fine at vets and doctors, unsure why, maybe because he knows they're only there for a short while?

Anyways that is why I think Rotisserie Chicken would be best off with me rather than another family / my friends original family, and haven't considered those options.

I now have Rotisserie Chicken napping in a bundle of A's clothes in my lap. He's barely ate or drank anything and has mostly slept.

I'm quite worried since Rotisserie Chicken typically eats and drinks anything he can get his paws on. Magically he's never had trouble drinking water.

He last ate yesterday, when according to eyewitness accounts, A handfed Rotisserie Chicken a Churru stick and put a bowl of food/water next to them and Rotisserie Chicken ate/drank it all + his other meals.

I'm told Rotisserie Chicken was right next to A as they passed away. Rotisserie Chicken is suffering heavily from grief in losing A.

Note: I've gotten Rotisserie Chicken's stuff and most of A's things too to aid them. This isn't the only place I'm looking for advice on and I'm researching too + contacting my vet friend. But I'd appreciate seeing anything helpful that can help Rotisserie Chicken adapt to my home that would be the most comfortable/least stressing for him.

edit: I forgot to mention that both my partner and I have considered getting a cat before. However since we know nothing about cats other than our experience with Rotisserie Chicken, we planned on setting some time at the end of the month to plan our how we would research on how to take care of cats for minimum half a yr. Rotisserie Chicken happened to appear a day before this plan went into action.

Leash training So I just bought two extra small dog harnesses to try and leash train my kitties. I have never done this before and was wondering if anyone has done some trial and error and has some tips to help me out?

Here’s my plan, please let me know what else I need to do:

First I’m getting them used to the harness indoors for 10-15 minutes a day, and using the time with the harness on as playtime with catnip and treats. My hope is they associate the harness with fun and playtime so they don’t hide or run when I bring out the harness. I’ve done this once, as I bought the harnesses today.

My next planned steps will be, once I can put the harness on without needing help holding the wiggly kitties still, and they just accept it as normal, I’ll let them drag a leash around. Then I’ll get them used to tension on the leash, and then move to outdoors.

Obviously this sounds good to me in theory, but is there anything I should be aware of, tips, things to look out for, or is it a good idea to leave the harness on unsupervised? I haven’t, but for future reference. Also taking them outside, one cat (4 y/o) grew up on a farm so she’s been out before but the other has been an apartment kitten her whole life (8 months.)

Thanks in advance!

Seeking Advice on Toilet Training Hi everyone! We are planning to adopt a 2.5 year old cat and she will be staying with us in a few weeks time. She has a peculiar problem of not using the litter box and we are keen for advice to better prepare ourselves for her arrival! We haven’t brought her to a vet but intend to bring her once she comes home to us.

• She was rescued from a hoarders house and lived with 39 other cats in a kitchen :( They did not have a steady supply of food and there were no litter boxes at all.

• Upon rescue, she was placed with an experience fosterer who runs a cat socialisation programme. She currently lives in their home and shares a big living room space with 3 kittens and 4 other adult cats. She has her own spots and prefers to keep her space from the other kitties. She's been with them for 2/3 months so far.

• The fosterer have tried many things to encourage her to use the litterbox, including using 6 different types of litter and even newspaper and pee pads. She continues to prefer to pee and poop in the toilet, next to a drain tile. She occasionally defecates in the kitchen sink. They initially also tried keeping her in a large crate with her litterbox, but she would defecate right next to it. When the fosterer attempts to put her in the box, we notice she looks scared and struggles or attempts to climb out immediately.

We would love to receive some tips and advice on how to help her with litter training especially since both of us work full time and will not be around all the time to clean up the mess. Another worry we have is that she will never learn how to use the litterbox given that so many strategies havent worked so far!

We plan to use pheromone tofu litter in a low walled stainless steel litterbox, and add some Fresh step cat attractant to it. We also plan to place her near or inside the litterbox and give her a treat as a reward. Would appreciate any thoughts on this!

Advice for helping new cat acclimate! Hello! My partner and I have just adopted our first cat together. Her name is Valentine and she's just over a year old.

We drove to a different city to pick her up and unfortunately her ride home was pretty rough, she cried the whole time and even grabbed hard onto the bars of her carrier and shook them a few times. We periodically fed her churu which calmed her briefly. She's been hiding under the bed since we brought her home ~5 hours ago, which we expected.

I've read that it's good to keep them in a single room for the first few days as to not overwhelm them. We live in a 1br apartment roughly 550sqft so it's not huge or anything. Regardless, we've been keeping her in the bedroom with access to food, water, litterbox, toys, a bed, and checking in periodically. I've been wondering if she'll be okay with it when we go to sleep in the bedroom later tonight? I don't want to do anything to scare or overwhelm her while she adjusts!

New cat acclimation question Hi all! We are going to be adopting a cat soon and I want to utilize our spare bedroom as the first step in making our kitty feel welcome in our apartment. My question is- is it ok to move the litter box after this acclimation period? We don’t plan to keep it in the spare bedroom, but instead in a hall closet that has no door. I don’t want to cause any confusion or risk accidents by moving it after the fact. Is it ok to still do this? Thanks!

My cat is sick Hi reddit. I have an old cat and he’s been peeing and pooping himself a lot. I’ve been to the vet already and they did some test and found nothing. I paid around 2k for all of it. I changed his good and it got better for a little bit but now it’s happening again. Things have been really hard for me, im struggling with some serious mental health issues and the price of everything has gone up in Canada and I just cannot afford to go back to the vet with him. He’s 17. Ive spend so much time cleaning after him, cancelling plans, not going to work because my appartement is covered in pee. Im so sad about it. My life quality is seriously impacted and i really dont wanna enthanize him but i cant keep going like this. Waking up in an appartement covered in poop is taking a toll on me and im already seeing a therapist for my depression every week. I dont know what to do, i found this cat outside during a snow storm 17 years ago and we’ve been together every day since. Advise would be welcome.

Help giving cat medication Recently, I've been required to give my cat ear and oral medication due to multiple health concerns. Usually when my cat needs medication it's only one pill which my partner and I can eventually get her to take, this time it's consistent medication over the course of 10 or so weeks. We've tried putting medication in her food, she won't eat the food. We've tried coating pills in every treat or food you can imagine, and she won't eat it. We've tried the purrito, she goes nuts and claws her way out of it. The second she sees a bottle of medication she runs under the bed and takes hours to get her out. We have run out of ideas on how to give her medication without stressing her out any more. We've tried when she's asleep and she wakes up when we go near her when she's recently been having to take medication. Does anyone have any tips for us? Thanks.

Help me train my friend's cat Hi everyone! I recently moved in with my friend for university and she has two cats and they're... a bit wild. Both were found as feral kittens and they're less than 2 years old I think, so still not too big. Both of them eat plants in the house when left unsupervised with one, which is a problem for me, because I have a lot of plants and I feel bad about them being chewed on all the time. They also have huge issues with food, whenever someone is making food in the kitchen they just jump on the counter every second and try to steal it, you throw them off, they're back not even a second later and nothing works on them, they don't feel guilty, they don't react to telling them "no" firmly (which usually works on my dog) or anything. My friend tried to train them out of bad behaviours, but I feel like she gave up a bit and I thought about trying since I live with them too now and I want more peace for both me and my friend. One of the cats is significantly worse by behaviour than the other, she's obsessed with bread and if she manages to get her paws on a piece of it she will literally growl and hold onto her dear life to that bread while scratching and biting anyone trying to take it away. I can't leave my room open cause they're biting my paintbrushes. If my friend gets treats for them they don't react to any attempts of training mostly, they're just focused on trying to take them. I don't know what to do, is there anyone specialising in cat behavioristics that could guide me on where to start?

How do you effectively train/discipline your cat? I have two cat babies, both rescues, both of whom I love immensely. One of them is just about the most easygoing cat I have ever been around. If he gets to sit in his daddy’s lap for a little while and has access to food, he is perfectly content.

The other one, however, I’m having some issues with. She’s a sweet girl but kind of needy, which is to be expected from any pet. I work from home now and it seems her neediness has gotten worse.

Specifically, she’s taken to coming to wake me up in the middle of the night for no reason. I get up, I check their bowls to make sure everything is good, have looked for other sources of her being bothered and come up with nothing. In addition to that, she started biting my feet and climbing all over my computer and stuff while I was trying to work. In order to avoid the distraction, I set up an office in the garage. The cats are not allowed in the garage as it is also my fiancé’s work shop so they get super dirty and track it all inside, as well as running the risk of them trying to eat a loose screw or something, so it’s just a cat free area. No matter what I do, she spends most of my work day sitting inside the garage door crying at me. It’s equally if not more distracting than what she was doing when I was inside.

I’m a writer so I really need to be able to focus while I’m working. Not only is it distracting while I’m working, but it’s hard to focus on anything when I’m being woken up every few hours for no reason. I play with her and give her tons of love during the day, we use laser pointers and string toys and if I’m inside hanging out I’ll give her a catnip toy. She has the other cat to play with and regularly does. I’ve tried putting pet block on the window sill where she likes to wake me up from and along the bottom of the garage door and it made zero impact. I’ve tried rewarding her with treats on the rare occasions she’s busied herself while I’m working and leaves me alone. I don’t use a spray bottle because I read somewhere it’s abusive and will make her scared of me.

I obviously don’t want her to fear me. I love her to pieces. But something has got to give. What else could I potentially do to teach her these behaviors aren’t okay?

I live in a small 1 bed 1 bath apartment, so i’m wondering if i should leave the doors open and allow her to explore on her own time? What’s better? Positive reinforcement training strategies needed! (reposted from a previous sub) So I have a (roughly) 9mo male neutered cat, Bento. He is extremely high energy, and has learned he can manipulate me by being annoying. We also have an 11yo senior female spayed cat, jade, that he has no boundaries with and plays too roughly with.

He is VERY food motivated thankfully, but I'm kind of stumped on specific situations I want to train him out of and would love some strategies if anyone has any to share!

Firstly, how do I train him to back off of something when I firmly say "NO"? And would investing in a clicker be worth it to couple with treats? And how do I prevent treat training from turning him into a treat fiend? lol

Scenario 1: bento is allowed on my desk to sit and nap, which I now wonder should not be allowed... However, between 4 and 5am, he likes to mess with and knock down things on my desk to make me get up and feed him. I can tell him NO and pull him off and lock him out of my room as much as I want, but he'll continue (I CANNOT keep him out of my room all night, my bathroom has his and Jade's litter box). How do I train him to stop doing this and wait for breakfast at 6am?

Scenario 2: Rough play with Jade. He wants to play, but jade doesn't like how he tackles her and gets too rough. It has been nearly two decades since I had a kitten or super young cat, so I am very rusty and a bit out of my depth here. Any and all constructive advice would be appreciated to help tame a Brat Cat. Again, he's highly food motivated, but stubborn, and isolating in timeout is VERY limited in my very tiny apartment.

Any tips for healthy cat? First time having a cat. She turns 1 in a few weeks. All I do is give food and toys. Not sure what foods are good to be honest I never got to conclusions. So I just do mix Purina one, Felix, gourmet, and wellness core dry as well.

Are there any supplements to keep her healthy? Such as urinary support, extra vitamins anything that might prevent problems before they even start. Something good for vision, any specific toothpaste and also any specific toothbrush since atm I just use a baby toothbrush. Just anything extra I can do for her

Are there any particular types of toys to keep her happy as she is used to then balls, mice, coils. Bought a bird that makes sound but didn't ever play with it.

How do I train her? I recently just got a kitten she’s been with me for 2 weeks now she is 10 weeks old and refuses any treat. I want to try training her the basic’s like touch and sit but she either gets distracted or doesn’t want the treats any tips??

People who live in loud, unpredictable cities, how did you acclimate your cat? We live next to the train, trolley, ballpark, and main drag of our city. Unexpected fireworks, protests, and the earthshattering boom of train carts slamming together at 3am are a constant in our apartment.

We recently fostered a 1 year old male cat and he started displaying some troubling symptoms. After every test under the sun he was diagnosed with Feline idiopathic cystitis (FIC). Basically stress makes his bladder become inflamed. We tried closing the windows, noise makers, running the AC and cat TV as well as CBD drops, Silvervine, extensive play sessions but nothing seemed to calm him down. The vet suggested we put him on gabapentin for him to continue living with us.

He's now back at the rescue in nice quiet suburbia but we are hesitant to bring another cat in just to have them be stressed.

How did you acclimate your cat to noisy living? Did you have them as a kitten and they just got used to it?

Cat Health Yesterday i adopted a cat from the shelter. They said he was a stray and estimated his age to be around 4 years old. He was castrated after arriving at the shelter.

He is very friendly from the beginning and had no problem using the litterbox, but i have some doubts about his health.

* After pooping his butt smells quite bad and some liquid poop stayed on his butt.
* he sheds A LOT of hair, even after lots of combing it does not become less.
He leaves tiny puddles of pee in random places.

I also believe he has a little trouble cleaning himself, i see him not do it very often as i see other cats do it.

What do i do? A visit to the vet is definitely a must, but if anyone has experience with these things i would love to hear about it.
